title: Opinion: Youth rage, burning bright. What hand could tame thy generational asymmetry?
html:
Claude Lavoie is a contributing columnist for The Globe and Mail. He was director-general of economic studies and policy analysis at the Department of Finance from 2008 to 2023.

This essay is part of the Prosperity’s Path series. In a time of geopolitical instability and a shifting world order, the challenges facing Canada's economy have only gotten more visible, numerous and intense. This series brings solutions.

From Paris to Montpellier, Madrid and Rome, young people across Europe are protesting. Hundreds of thousands storm the streets, and while they’re largely peaceful, looting and vandalism abound. Shops are boarding up windows. A French teen lost his hand. “If we burn, you burn with us,” so reads their unofficial slogan.

This may seem far away and foreign. But the Gen Z protesters’ grievances are familiar: class inequality and a growing feeling that their generation is forced to put in more than its share. This tension can be seen in Canada too.

Think tanks such as Generation Squeeze argue that public finances tilt too far toward older generations. This month, university and college students in Ontario walked out of class to protest the province’s cuts to tuition assistance. The latest federal budget made progress in many areas, but it did little to ease the burden on future generations.

Protesters march in Bordeaux, France, on Saturday, the latest in a series of nationwide demonstrations about the rising cost of living and inequality organized by the Yellow Vest movement, labour unions and high school and university students.CHRISTOPHE ARCHAMBAULT/AFP/Getty Images

Reforms made in the 1990s to our pensions and public finances have made Canada better positioned to confront a greyer world. But our fiscal position has deteriorated since then, and the budget shows it is not expected to improve, leaving the next generation with a heavier load. Many programs still channel resources to older Canadians that could do more good if spent on younger ones.

The pressures will only grow. Fertility is projected to stay well below replacement level. According to the C.D. Howe Institute, the ratio of seniors to working-age people will rise to close to 50 per cent in 2070 from about 30 per cent today, at the current immigration rate.

Raising immigration is not a sustainable solution. Immigrants age too, and the scale needed to keep this ratio from growing would exceed our capacity to integrate newcomers. Population aging strains any pay-as-you-go program that mainly benefits older people, since fewer people pay in while more draw out. Public pensions and health care are prime examples.

What can Canada do?

Across-the-board cuts in these programs are not the answer. Cutting health care services affects every generation and creates inequities within each one. The same goes for public pensions such as Old Age Security and the Guaranteed Income Supplement.

Shifting OAS money wholesale to youth programs would give young people more now but less when they are old, leaving them no richer over a lifetime. Today’s seniors would lose, and the hardest hit would be people with low incomes or precarious jobs, who rely on OAS the most, while their children would shoulder more of their support.

Raising the eligibility age from 65 to 67, as the Harper government tried, would keep some people in the work force longer, but it would be those with no financial choice, often working in physically punishing jobs. We enjoy more healthy years in retirement than past generations did, but we are also richer and can reasonably afford to spend part of that wealth on leisure.

Canada should rebalance its spending toward younger generations, but by targeting higher-income seniors and fixing tax and program design rather than broad-based program cuts. Many studies show that inequalities are larger within than across generations.

There is a strong case for raising the OAS clawback rate for those making above a certain amount – shifting funding away from OAS but in a more targeted way. Opponents warn that it discourages work by imposing further costs on people who make more, but studies show the effect is tiny for higher earners. Ottawa could raise the rate only above a certain income threshold and leave the rate for lower-income seniors untouched.

Statistics Canada reports that seniors’ poverty is 5.4 per cent, compared with 7.9 per cent for core working-age people, 11 per cent for youth and 31.4 per cent for single working-age adults. It is hard to justify sending OAS cheques to people who earn more than the average worker.

Tax parameters deserve a look too. What is the rationale for the pension or age tax credit, these broad-based benefits to seniors? At the very least, we could claw the latter back more aggressively for people making above a certain amount or limit its efficacy by restricting the credit to employment income. And why don’t TFSA withdrawals count toward OAS calculations for the clawback, when so much of what sits in those accounts is untaxed investment gains? These changes would make the system fairer and cheaper.

Another good option is to expand the Canada Pension Plan further. CPP is fully funded, meaning each generation contributes for its own retirement. Seniors’ poverty may be low, but middle-class workers without an employer plan can avoid poverty yet still face a steep drop in income at retirement. CPP replaces only a third of working income, and only up to a limit.

A more generous CPP could guarantee every Canadian an adequate pension, protected against inflation and longevity risk. OAS would then serve as a top-up for those who mostly worked low-wage jobs or were self-employed. This would also significantly reduce the pressure on OAS and GIS.

Bigger tax changes could also be considered. Consumption is more stable than income over a person’s life, so lowering personal levies and increasing the goods and services tax, shifting the tax burden from income tax to consumption, would reduce the effect of aging on the tax base and limit loopholes.

Canada does not currently have an inheritance tax; a progressive inheritance tax could improve equality of opportunity. Canada also does not tax primary residences; taxing capital gains on land or house value (maybe above some threshold) could lower prices, reduce speculation in housing and raise revenues in a fair way.

Protestors march through the streets of Vancouver in opposition to AI and the proposed local data centre projects associated with the technology, in June.DARRYL DYCK/The Canadian Press

The fiscal savings could be reallocated where needs are more pressing. Displaced workers, especially long-tenured ones, will need help as AI and trade tensions reshape the economy. Vulnerable seniors deserve support too. Rent and heating bills don’t shrink when a spouse dies, so widows should receive extra funds to offset part of the OAS (and often the Guaranteed Income Supplement as well) they lose.

On health care, some type of user fee, at least on non-preventive care, which could be income-tested, would make the system more sustainable and fairer between generations.

We could also do more to protect our environmental capital and ensure the revenues from it benefit future generations. Government inaction on climate change is one of the most prominent complaints among youth worldwide.

Ultimately, we must improve our institutions so that policies are evaluated for their long-term generational impact. It is far from clear that many of the recently announced budget measures will have significant effects on economic growth and future generations, despite the debt burden it leaves them.

Any policy should balance the needs of young and old without hurting fairness within each generation. The challenge is that governments are tempted to favour older, as well as richer, voters, whose share of the electorate and political influence keep growing.
summary: Canada should rebalance its spending toward younger generations, but by targeting higher-income seniors and fixing tax and program design rather than broad-based program cuts
